tier.0: One obvious edit with no design choice left in it. A typo, a rename inside one file, a constant, a docstring. If two reasonable engineers would produce the same diff, it is tier 0.
tier.1: A contained change to one subsystem. A few files, an existing pattern to follow, and a test that is obvious to write. The work is in doing it correctly, not in deciding what to do.
tier.2: The approach is the hard part, or the change crosses subsystems. Architecture, migrations, concurrency, security, releases, and anything where choosing wrong costs more than implementing slowly.

blast.low: Wrong is cheap and local. One file or module, no callers outside it, no data touched, nothing a user sees.
blast.medium: Wrong breaks callers inside this repo. A subsystem with internal consumers; the tests catch it, but more than one place moves.
blast.high: Wrong escapes the repo or cannot be caught by tests alone. Public API, stored data, credentials, CI, releases, or anything a user or another service depends on.

rubric.reversible: True when `git revert` alone puts the world back. False when the change writes or destroys data, migrates a schema, rotates a credential, or publishes something others can already have consumed. Reversibility is about the world, not about the diff.
rubric.ties: When cues disagree, take the higher tier: under-spending on a hard task costs a wrong answer, over-spending costs tokens. Tier and blast are independent — a one-line change to a shared default is tier 0 and blast medium. An irreversible task is never tier 0 and never blast low, however small its diff.
